sections.title: Form and substrate
sections.text: Pleomassaria siparia is a microscopic saprotrophic ascomycete recorded on dead wood, especially birch twigs (Betula). Its black ascomata occur scattered or in small groups, first immersed in the bark and sometimes showing through a minute slit or small swelling. They are depressed-globose and ostiolate; the type-material description gives a diameter of about 0.44–0.74 mm.

sections.title: Microscopic characters
sections.text: Each ascoma contains bitunicate, fissitunicate asci and brown, muriform ascospores (with transverse and longitudinal septa) that are constricted at the septa. A morphological and phylogenetic account reports typically 5–7 transverse septa and a longitudinal septum in several cells; measurements vary among descriptions and specimens. Microscopic examination is needed for identification.

sections.title: Ecology and limits
sections.text: Published records concern mainly dead Betula twigs, including B. pendula and B. pubescens, with occasional reports from other woody hosts. One study distinguished two biological species that cannot be told apart in the teleomorph; both were found on dead twigs of these two birches, so field identification may not separate the lineages. Birch is a frequently documented host, not an exclusive character. No consistent fruiting season is established here. Its phylogenetic placement within Pleosporales has been discussed; this entry retains the name Pleomassaria siparia used by the taxonomic databases consulted.

traits: Microscopic saprotrophic ascomycete on dead wood, frequently recorded on birch twigs
Black ascomata, scattered or in small groups, immersed in bark and later slightly exposed; depressed-globose and ostiolate
Bitunicate asci; brown, muriform ascospores constricted at the septa
Diagnostic characters are microscopic; a single general photograph is not sufficient for reliable identification
safetyNote: Food status has not been assessed; this entry does not recommend consumption. The illustration is explanatory, with enlarged microscopic views that are not to scale; it is not a micrograph or an identification key.
